title: Two ways, and the love that gives
sum: The book opens with its long title, "The teaching of the Lord through the twelve apostles to the Gentiles," and its theme: "There are two ways, one of life and one of death." The way of life is love of the God who made you and of your neighbor, with the Golden Rule in its negative form. A block of sayings close to the Sermon on the Mount and Luke's Sermon on the Plain then spells it out: bless those who curse you, turn the other cheek, go the second mile, give to anyone who asks. The chapter ends with a warning to those who take gifts they do not need, and a saying found in no Gospel: "Let your alms sweat in your hands."
readings: The two ways and the two great commandments are Jewish teaching (Deuteronomy 30:15-19; Jeremiah 21:8; Leviticus 19:18). Lake reports that many scholars think the original Two Ways was a Jewish document for teaching converts. On this reading the sayings of 1:3-6 are a Christian layer laid over an older Jewish lesson.
Read as Jesus' teaching for Gentiles

The title presents the whole as "the teaching of the Lord." The sayings of 1:3-5 are Jesus' own, from the Sermon on the Mount, and the chapter shows Gentile converts being taught his way of love from the start.

views.H: The title is probably later than the material under it, and 1:3-2:1 is missing from Barnabas's Two Ways and the Latin one; Kraft thinks it "most probable" that it was added at one of the latest stages. Lake's footnote at 1:5 thinks that part later than Hermas (about AD 140).
views.J: The two ways, the love commands and the negative Golden Rule (Tobit 4:15) are all at home in Jewish teaching; the chapter reads like a Jewish catechism for converts, with the words of Jesus added.
views.N: The sayings of 1:3-5 mix Matthew 5:39-48 and Luke 6:27-35, with additions ("fast for the people who persecute you"; "you will have no enemy"). They are the main evidence in the argument over whether the Didache knew written Gospels.
views.L: This is teaching for people before baptism (7:1): moral formation comes first. Kraft calls the Two Ways "the material for prebaptismal instruction."

deep.b: The Didache's Two Ways runs smoothly from "Now the way of life is this" (1:2) to "The teaching's second commandment is this" (2:1) and the commandments of 2:2. Between them stands 1:3-6, a block of Jesus' sayings with its own heading ("The teaching of these words is this"). Barnabas 18-20, which shares the rest of the Two Ways, has nothing like it. Nor does the Latin Two Ways, and the Georgian version lacks 1:5-6. So Kraft takes 1:3b-2:1 as "a Christian contribution that may have been added by the Didachist himself." Inside the block, 1:5 also stands in Hermas's Commandment 2 (Shepherd of Hermas 27:4–6), and 1:6 seems to pull against 1:5 (give to all; but let your alms sweat until you know whom to give to). The Plain English Translation translates the block as the manuscript gives it.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the two halves of 1:5-6 answer two kinds of asking
deep.b: This is my suggestion. "Keep giving to anyone who asks you" (1:5) and "Let your alms sweat in your hands until you know who you are giving to" (1:6) may answer two different situations in the same church: the poor neighbor who asks for bread, and the traveler who arrives asking for support. Chapters 11-13 give exactly that second case its own tests (one or two days, no money, work if you stay). On this reading 1:6 is not a contradiction but a bridge to the later rules for visitors. The tension can also be explained as two sources set side by side.

echoes: Deuteronomy 30:15-19; Jeremiah 21:8; Matthew 22:37-39; Matthew 7:12; Matthew 5:38-48; Luke 6:27-35; 1 Peter 2:11; Barnabas 18:1; Sirach 12:1

settings.by: An unnamed writer or editor, in the name of the Lord and the Twelve
settings.to: Gentile converts and the churches that taught them
settings.when: Set over the book by the time of the one complete manuscript (copied 1056); when it was first added is not known
settings.why: To claim the book's teaching as the Lord's, handed on by the apostles, for non-Jews coming to faith. Knowing it is a title, not a signature, keeps the reader from taking it as a claim that the Twelve wrote it.
settings.readers: The book's first readers were Gentile converts (the title: "to the Gentiles") being taught before baptism (7:1: "First say all these things, then baptize"). Where they lived is argued: Robert A. Kraft (Anchor Bible Dictionary, quoted at Early Christian Writings) reports that most commentators favor Syria (Audet; Hazelden Walker; Rordorf and Tuilier) or Syro-Palestine (Niederwimmer), with Egypt (Kraft) and Asia Minor (Vokes) also proposed.

settings.by: A teacher, speaking as to a child ("my child," 3:1)
settings.why: To set out the way of life and the way of death so the learner knows what life as a Christian requires before being baptized. Read as a catechism, the lists are not a complete ethic but the basics every convert must know.
settings.readers: A single learner ("my child," 3:1) who has not yet been baptized (7:1). Kraft calls the Two Ways "the material for prebaptismal instruction"; Lake, teaching "to be taught to catechumens before their baptism."
views: Lake reports that many think the original Two Ways was a Jewish pre-Christian document used to teach converts, perhaps proselytes; on this view the first hearers of its core were Gentiles joining Israel.
Whatever its origin, the text as it stands is Christian: it calls itself the Lord's teaching and quotes Jesus.

title: The second commandment
sum: "The teaching's second commandment" is love of neighbor turned into a list of things not to do. It begins with the Ten Commandments in Jesus' order (murder, adultery, stealing, false testimony, craving) and adds the sins of a Greek city: the sexual abuse of boys, magic and potions, abortion and the killing of newborns. Then it moves inward, to words and attitudes: no false oaths, no slander, no grudges, no double tongue, no greed or pride, no plotting. It ends with a command that turns the list positive: hate no one, but correct some, pray for some, and love some more than yourself.

views.H: The list has the same items as Barnabas 19, in a different and more orderly arrangement. Lake's three possibilities for the Two Ways (Barnabas used the Didache, the reverse, or both a common source) leave open which form of these lines is older.
views.J: The list reads like the commandments applied for Gentile converts; Josephus says the Law forbids abortion (Against Apion 2.202).
views.N: The order of the first commands matches Matthew 19:18 and Romans 13:9, and "You must not swear falsely" is Matthew 5:33's Greek.
views.L: Churches cite 2:2 in their teaching on abortion; the site's card at Jeremiah 1 gives how several do, and the Orthodox row there quotes this verse.

echoes: Exodus 20:13-17; Matthew 19:18-19; Romans 13:9; Matthew 5:33; Leviticus 19:17-18; Barnabas 19:4-5

settings.what: The second commandment: love of neighbor
settings.by: The teacher of the Two Ways
settings.when: As part of the Two Ways
settings.why: To make plain to converts from pagan life which practices the love of neighbor rules out, including some that Greek thinkers accepted (Aristotle proposed exposing deformed infants and early abortion, Politics 7, 1335b), as well as the abuse of boys and magic.
settings.readers: Gentile converts (the title) being taught, before baptism, what love of neighbor forbids, from murder and theft to abortion, magic and the abuse of boys.

title: My child: small sins and great ones
sum: Five sayings, each addressed to "my child," trace a great sin back to the small ones that lead to it: anger to murder; desire, foul talk and a roving eye to adultery; omens, spells and astrology to idol worship; lying, love of money and vanity to theft; complaining, stubbornness and evil thoughts to blasphemy. Then the positive: be gentle, "since the gentle will inherit the earth" (3:7, the Beatitude of Matthew 5:5), be patient, merciful and quiet, tremble at the words you have heard, keep company with the lowly, and accept whatever happens as good, "knowing that without God nothing happens."

views.J: "Make a fence round the Torah" (Mishnah Avot 1:1): the sayings keep the learner far from the line by forbidding what leads to it. The address "my child" is the voice of Proverbs and Sirach.
views.N: The pattern matches Jesus' teaching that anger and the lustful look already break the commandments (Matthew 5:21-28), and 3:7 nearly quotes the Beatitude of the gentle, without "Blessed."
views.H: Barnabas 19 has many of the same lines but not the five-part "fence" pattern, which is the Didache's own.

echoes: Matthew 5:5; Psalm 37:11; Matthew 5:21-28; Isaiah 66:2; Romans 12:16; Matthew 10:29; Proverbs 1:8

settings.by: The teacher, as a father to a son
settings.when: As part of the Two Ways
settings.why: To train habits, not only to forbid deeds: the learner is shown how small faults grow into great sins, and which virtues to grow instead.
settings.readers: The single learner called "my child" (3:1-6), a convert who has not yet been baptized (7:1).

title: Teachers, peace, giving and the household
sum: The learner is to honor whoever speaks God's word "as the Lord," seek out the saints every day, make peace, judge fairly, and not be double-minded. A long section on giving follows: do not hold out your hands to take and pull them back to give; give from your labor "as ransom for your sins"; do not grumble; share everything with your brother, "for if you are partners in what never dies, how much more in the things that die?" Then a short household code: teach your children to fear God; do not order slaves about in bitterness; slaves, submit as to a figure of God. The way of life ends with confession "in the church" and coming to prayer with a clean conscience.

views.J: Giving as ransom for sin (Daniel 4:27; Tobit 12:9; Sirach 3:30) and the rule against adding to or taking from the commandments (Deuteronomy 4:2) are Jewish teaching kept in full.
views.N: The sharing of goods echoes Acts 4:32, the household code Ephesians 6 and Colossians 3-4, confession James 5:16.
views.L: 4:14 asks for confession of sins in the gathered church; the Didache does not say to whom or how. The site's card at Psalm 32 gives the churches' views on confession.

echoes: Acts 4:32; Sirach 4:31; Daniel 4:27; Tobit 12:9; Ephesians 6:4-9; Deuteronomy 4:2; James 5:16; Barnabas 19:5-12

settings.by: The teacher of the Two Ways
settings.to: The learner, now addressed as a member of a household and a church
settings.when: As part of the Two Ways
settings.why: To bring the learner into the life of the community: honoring teachers, keeping peace, sharing goods, ruling a household, and confessing sins together. It shows that the way of life is lived in a church, not alone.
settings.readers: Converts who would soon take their place in a house church with masters and slaves, parents and children.

title: The way of death
sum: "But the way of death is this." Twenty-two sins in a row, from murders and adulteries to boasting, then a portrait of the people who walk that way: they persecute the good, love lies, do not know the reward of righteousness, show no mercy to the poor, do not know the one who made them, murder children and destroy "what God has formed," turn away the needy, and side with the rich against the poor. The chapter ends with a prayer for the learners: "Children, may you be rescued from all these!"

views.H: Barnabas 20 has a shorter, differently ordered list and the same portrait almost word for word; the two clearly share a source or one used the other.
views.N: Vice lists like this stand in Romans 1:29-31, Galatians 5:19-21 and Mark 7:21-22; the site uses its New Testament renderings for the shared words.
views.J: The sins against the poor, the widow and the needy are the prophets' charges (Isaiah 1:23; Amos 2:6-7).

echoes: Matthew 15:19; Mark 7:21-22; Romans 1:29-31; Galatians 5:19-21; Isaiah 1:23; Barnabas 20:1-2

settings.when: As the close of the Two Ways
settings.why: To show, by contrast, what the learner is leaving behind, and to end the lesson with a prayer for rescue.
settings.readers: The learners together, now called "children" (5:2), at the close of their teaching before baptism.

title: The Lord's yoke
sum: A short close to the Two Ways: let no one lead you away from this teaching. "For if you can carry the whole yoke of the Lord, you will be perfect. But if you cannot, do what you can." On food, too, carry what you can; but keep strictly away from food sacrificed to idols, "for it is the worship of dead gods."

views.H: "The whole yoke" may mean all of Jesus' teaching just given, or the whole Jewish Law, which Gentiles may take on as far as they can. The food rule matches the apostles' decree of Acts 15.
views.J: "Yoke" is a Jewish picture for the Law; the chapter may preserve a teaching for God-fearing Gentiles who kept part of the Law.
views.N: Jesus' "my yoke is kind to wear" (Matthew 11:29-30), Peter's yoke too heavy to carry (Acts 15:10) and the decree against idol food (Acts 15:29) all stand behind these verses.
views.L: 6:2 makes room for growth: the standard is full, and the learner does what he can.

echoes: Matthew 11:29-30; Acts 15:10; Acts 15:28-29; Matthew 5:48; 1 Corinthians 8:1-13; 1 Thessalonians 1:9

settings.what: The close of the Two Ways
settings.why: To warn against other teachers and to set the one firm food rule for Gentile converts, while allowing for weakness in the rest.
settings.readers: Gentile converts who were being asked what of the Jewish Law they must keep, as in Acts 15; Kraft thinks 6:3 reflects "Jewish-Christian interest" in food laws for Gentiles.

title: Baptism
sum: The church order begins. "About baptism, baptize like this." First teach all the Two Ways; then baptize "into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, in living water," that is, running water. If there is none, other water; cold, or if not, warm; and if there is not enough of either, pour water three times on the head. The one who baptizes, the one being baptized and any others who can should fast beforehand, the candidate for one or two days. Kraft calls the permission to pour "probably the earliest reference to that practice in Christianity."

views.H: The rules show baptism in rural or small-town settings where a stream or spring was preferred but not always to hand. The threefold name is Matthew 28:19's.
views.J: "Living water" was required in some purifications of the Law (Leviticus 14:5; 15:13); the preference for living water may come from that background.
views.N: The words match Matthew 28:19; Acts speaks of baptism "in the name of Jesus Christ" (Acts 2:38). Fasting goes with baptism as in Acts 9:9 and 13:2-3.
views.L: The chapter can be read as permission to pour or as proof that immersion was the rule; the site's cards at Acts 8 (immersion) and Matthew 28 (the words) give each tradition's view, and this page does not repeat them.

echoes: Matthew 28:19; Acts 2:38; Acts 8:36-39; John 4:10; Acts 9:9; Acts 13:2-3; Romans 6:3-4

settings.by: The writer of the church order
settings.to: Whoever baptizes in the community ("you" singular in 7:2-4)
settings.when: When a learner has been taught the Two Ways
settings.why: To say how to baptize properly and what to do when the ideal is not possible. It shows the church caring for the right form and the right words while bending on the amount and temperature of the water.
settings.readers: The one who baptizes ("you" singular in 7:2-4) and the candidates, who have heard the Two Ways and fast for a day or two first (7:1, 4).

title: Fasting and prayer
sum: "Your fasts must not be with the hypocrites," who fast on Monday and Thursday; fast on Wednesday and Friday. "And do not pray like the hypocrites": pray as the Lord commanded in his good news, and the Lord's Prayer follows in a form very close to Matthew's, ending with "For yours is the power and the glory forever." "Pray like this three times a day."

views.H: Kraft notes that the Wednesday and Friday fasts "were widely observed in early Christianity" and that this doxology "seems to have been known in Egypt ... and Syria." The Didache seems to know Matthew's form of the prayer, or the church's spoken form of it.
views.J: The chapter keeps prayer three times a day (Mishnah Berakhot 4:1 sets morning, afternoon and evening prayers) and fasting twice a week (Luke 18:12), but by design on other days. Kraft takes Monday and Thursday as the "(Pharisaic) Jewish fasts," and "the hypocrites," Matthew's word, as Pharisees or practicing Jews.
views.N: Matthew 6 joins giving, prayer and fasting against "the hypocrites"; the Didache takes the same three and gives Matthew's prayer.
views.L: The site's cards at Matthew 6 and Judith 8 ask whether Christians should keep fixed fast days.

echoes: Matthew 6:5-18; Luke 11:2-4; Luke 18:12; Daniel 6:10; Psalm 55:17; Acts 3:1; Acts 10:9

settings.what: Rules for fasting and the Lord's Prayer
settings.by: The writer of the church order
settings.why: To give the church its own rhythm of fasting and prayer, distinct from "the hypocrites," and to make the Lord's Prayer its fixed daily prayer.
settings.readers: A community living near Jews and keeping Jewish customs, which needed to mark its own identity; who exactly "the hypocrites" were is argued (see the note at 8:1).
views: Kraft: the saying "originally may have referred to Pharisaic practices (cf. Matt. 23:13), although the Didachist might mean simply practicing Jews."
The words would also fit Christians who still fasted with the synagogue, so that the rule draws a line inside the church.

title: The thanksgiving over cup and bread
sum: "About the thanksgiving, give thanks like this." First over the cup: thanks "for the holy vine of your servant David, which you made known to us through your servant Jesus." Then over the broken bread: thanks "for the life and knowledge," and a prayer that, as the bread's grain was scattered on the mountains and made one, the church be gathered from the ends of the earth into God's kingdom. Only the baptized may eat or drink, for the Lord said, "Do not give what is holy to the dogs."
readings: The meal is "the thanksgiving," holy, limited to the baptized, with a cup and broken bread; on this reading it is the church's Eucharist in an early form, centered on thanks rather than on the words of institution.

The prayers say nothing of Jesus' body and blood or death, the order is cup then bread, and 10:1 says "after you have eaten your fill"; on this reading 9-10 is a community meal, with the Lord's Supper either following (10:6) or in chapter 14.

views.H: Whether chapters 9-10 are the Lord's Supper, a love feast, or something else is the main question. Kraft: "At first glance they seem to represent a 'Eucharist' liturgy," but the meal of 10:1, the silence about Jesus' body and blood, and the separate rite of 14:1 led "many commentators" to a love feast; he himself places the prayers at a yearly service for the newly baptized. Lake's footnote compares the shorter text of Luke 22.
views.J: The prayers follow the shape of Jewish table blessings: the Mishnah gives blessings over wine ("Who creates fruit of the vine") and bread (Mishnah Berakhot 6:1), speaks of wine blessed "before the meal" (Mishnah Berakhot 6:5), and has a blessing after eating (chapter 10). The themes, the vine, David, the gathering of the scattered, are Israel's.
views.N: The cup before the bread stands in Luke 22:17-19 and 1 Corinthians 10:16; "one loaf" and "one body" in 1 Corinthians 10:17; "what is holy to the dogs" is Matthew 7:6.
views.L: Only the baptized share the meal (9:5); Kraft links this to the meal that followed baptism, "from which all nonbaptized persons were excluded"; the site's card at Matthew 7 asks whether communion should be open or closed today.

deep.h: What the meal prayers say, and do not say
deep.b: The prayers of chapters 9-10 are short and full of Jewish images: the vine of David, God's name living in the heart, the scattered grain made one loaf, the church gathered from the four winds, "Hosanna to the God of David." They give thanks for "life and knowledge," "knowledge and faith and immortality," "spiritual food and drink, and eternal life." They call Jesus God's "servant" (pais), as the prayers of Acts 4 do. They do not quote "This is my body" or speak of Jesus' blood or death, and they put the cup first. These features are the evidence in the debate over what the meal was, which Kraft sets out (see the views above). The Apostolic Constitutions, rewriting the prayers in the 300s, keeps the grain "once scattered, and is now become one loaf," but adds thanks for Jesus' suffering, death and resurrection and for his blood, calls him God's "Son," and gives the freedom of 10:7 to presbyters (book 7, chapters 25-26, in the Ante-Nicene Fathers translation; the New Advent page prints the first as "XXXV"). It also adds a thanksgiving over ointment (chapter 27), which the Coptic fragment has too, though the Greek manuscript and the Georgian version lack it (Kraft).

Lake's footnote says the order "first the Cup" is found elsewhere only in "the earliest text" of Luke 22:17 and following, and perhaps in 1 Corinthians 10:16. Lake probably meant the shorter text of Luke (in Codex Bezae and some Old Latin copies, with one cup before the bread), since he says it "omits v. 20"; the site's Luke follows the longer text of nearly all manuscripts, which has a cup before the bread and another after supper (see the notes and variants at Luke 22:17-20). Either way, Luke and Paul show that a cup before the bread was known.

echoes: Luke 22:17-20; 1 Corinthians 10:16-17; 1 Corinthians 11:23-26; Matthew 7:6; Psalm 80:8; John 15:1; Acts 4:25-27; Isaiah 11:12

settings.by: The writer of the church order, giving prayers for the community
settings.to: The gathered church, who speak the prayers to God ("We thank you, our Father")
settings.why: To give the church words of thanks over cup and bread that tie the meal to Jesus, David's line and the hope of the gathered church, and to keep the meal holy by limiting it to the baptized.
settings.readers: Only the baptized (9:5): the assembled church, which says the prayers together.
views: Kraft: "At first glance they seem to represent a 'Eucharist' liturgy."
Kraft reports that the meal of 10:1 and the separate rite of 14:1 "led many commentators to suggest" a love feast; G. Dix (1945) read it so.
Kraft's own view: prayers from a love feast, used at a yearly service where the newly baptized shared their first Eucharist.

title: After the meal: Marana tha
sum: "After you have eaten your fill, give thanks like this." The longer prayer thanks the holy Father for his name living in their hearts and for knowledge, faith and immortality; praises the almighty Master who made all things and gave food to all, but "to us" spiritual food and drink and eternal life; asks him to remember his church, rescue it, perfect it and gather it from the four winds into his kingdom. It ends in short cries: "Let grace come, and let this world pass away. Hosanna to the God of David! Whoever is holy, let him come. Whoever is not, let him repent. Marana tha! Amen." Prophets may give thanks as much as they want.

views.H: "After you have eaten your fill" points to a full meal. Whether 10:6 is the call to the Lord's Supper itself is argued.
views.J: The order follows Jewish practice: a longer blessing after the meal (Mishnah Berakhot 7:3), with thanks for food and for God's name and a prayer for the gathering of his people.
views.N: "Spiritual food and drink" is 1 Corinthians 10:3-4; the four winds are Matthew 24:31; "Hosanna" Matthew 21:9 (where the crowd says "Son of David"; see the variant at 10:6); "Marana tha" 1 Corinthians 16:22 and Revelation 22:20.
views.L: The prophets' freedom (10:7) shows written prayers used alongside free prayer; later the Apostolic Constitutions gave that freedom to presbyters.

echoes: 1 Corinthians 10:3-4; Matthew 24:31; Matthew 21:9; 1 Corinthians 16:22; Revelation 22:17-20; John 1:14; Acts 4:24

settings.by: The writer of the church order
settings.to: The gathered church, speaking to God; the last line (10:7) to the community about its prophets
settings.why: To close the meal with thanks for creation and salvation and with the church's longing for the Lord's coming, and to leave room for prophets to pray freely.
settings.readers: The same baptized assembly, now after eating (10:1), with its prophets free to give thanks as they wish (10:7).

title: Testing teachers, apostles and prophets
sum: Welcome whoever comes and teaches all these things; but not a teacher who undoes them. Traveling apostles are to be welcomed as the Lord, but may stay only a day or two and take only bread for the road; one who stays three days or asks for money is a false prophet. A prophet speaking in the Spirit is not to be tested or judged; yet not everyone who speaks in the Spirit is a prophet, only one who has "the Lord's ways." A prophet who orders a meal and eats it, does not do what he teaches, or asks money for himself is false. A tested prophet who acts out "an earthly mystery of the church" is left to God's judgment.

views.H: The chapter shows a stage of church life when traveling apostles and prophets still came and went, and churches needed simple tests against abuse. Lake: the Didache's "apostle" is a traveling missionary, not one of the Twelve.
views.N: Jesus' rules for his messengers (Matthew 10:9-11, 40-41), the warning "You will know who they are from their fruit" (Matthew 7:16), and the sin against the Spirit (Matthew 12:31) lie behind it; Paul's churches also had prophets weighed by others (1 Corinthians 14:29).
views.L: Whether there are still apostles and prophets is asked in the site's card at Ephesians 4.

deep.b: 11:7 forbids testing a prophet speaking in the Spirit, while 11:8-12 lists ways to know a false prophet, and 12:1 says to test every newcomer. The Didache's answer is in 11:8: a prophet is known "by their ways," his manner of life. The church does not sit in judgment on inspired words, but it watches whether the speaker lives like the Lord: does he stay too long, ask for money, eat what he orders, practice what he teaches? The same balance stands in Jesus' warning about false prophets: "You will know who they are from their fruit" (Matthew 7:16).

echoes: Matthew 10:9-11; Matthew 10:40-41; Matthew 7:15-20; Matthew 12:31-32; 1 Corinthians 14:29; 1 John 4:1; 2 John 1:10; Acts 13:1-3

settings.what: Rules for teachers, apostles and prophets
settings.by: The writer of the church order
settings.when: Whenever a traveling teacher, apostle or prophet arrives
settings.why: To protect the church from false teachers and from people living off its welcome, without quenching the Spirit. Knowing these were small communities visited by strangers explains the simple tests of days and money.
settings.readers: Communities on travel routes visited by itinerant preachers, before settled local leaders had taken over their work (15:1-2).

title: Travelers and Christ-peddlers
sum: "Everyone who comes in the Lord's name is to be welcomed" and then tested. A traveler passing through is to be helped, but may stay only two or three days. One who wants to settle and has a trade must work for his food; one without a trade must be helped to find work, "so that no Christian will live idle among you." One who will not work is "a Christ-peddler."

views.H: The rules show networks of Christians traveling between towns and settling, and the strain this put on small churches.
views.N: Paul's "Whoever does not want to work should not eat either" (2 Thessalonians 3:10) and his refusal to be a burden (1 Thessalonians 2:9) say the same.
views.L: The chapter is an early example of a church organizing help for newcomers while guarding against freeloading.

echoes: Psalm 118:26; Matthew 21:9; 2 Thessalonians 3:10-12; Ephesians 4:28; 2 Corinthians 2:17; Acts 11:26

settings.by: The writer of the church order
settings.when: When any Christian arrives from elsewhere
settings.why: To keep the duty of welcome while preventing abuse, and to fold settlers into the church's working life.
settings.readers: Local churches that took in Christian travelers, some with a trade and some without (12:3-4).

title: Firstfruits for the prophets
sum: A true prophet or teacher who settles in a church "has earned his food," like the worker of Jesus' saying. So the firstfruits of winepress and threshing floor, of cattle and sheep, are to go to the prophets, "for they are your high priests"; if there is no prophet, to the poor. The same goes for bread, a jar of wine or oil, silver, clothing and anything else: give the first part "as the commandment says."

views.J: The firstfruits the Law gave the priests (Numbers 18:12-13; Deuteronomy 18:4) are given to the prophets; the chapter reads like the Torah's offerings carried into a Gentile church.
views.N: "A worker has earned his food" (Matthew 10:10) and Paul's argument that those who serve the altar share in it (1 Corinthians 9:13-14) stand behind the rule.
views.L: Calling prophets "high priests" gives Christian ministers a priestly title. Kraft: "The ancient high priests are replaced by the prophets"; later forms of this tradition put "bishop" and other clergy here. The site's cards at Hebrews 7 and 1 Peter 2 give the churches' views on priesthood.

settings.what: Support for resident prophets and teachers
settings.by: The writer of the church order
settings.to: Each household ("you" singular in 13:3-7) and the community
settings.when: At harvest and whenever food, wine, oil or goods are newly opened or gained
settings.why: To provide for prophets and teachers who settle, and for the poor, by an old and familiar practice. It shows the church treating its prophets as the Law treated its priests.
settings.readers: Farming households in a small church; Kraft thinks the farm produce of 13:3-7 points to "a semirural rather than a large urban environment."

title: The Lord's day
sum: "On the Lord's day of the Lord, when you have gathered, break bread and give thanks." First confess your wrongs, so that "your sacrifice" is pure; anyone with a quarrel must stay away until he has made peace, so that the sacrifice is not made unclean. For this is the sacrifice the Lord spoke of: "In every place and time, present to me a pure sacrifice. For I am a great king, says the Lord, and my name is wonderful among the nations."

views.H: Kraft takes "the Lord's (Day) of the Lord" as "probably" the regular Sunday meeting; C. W. Dugmore argued that only Easter is meant. Kraft also warns that "prayers and praise often were called 'sacrifices'" in this period. Whether this meal is the same as the one in chapters 9-10 is argued.
views.J: The quotation joins Malachi 1:11 and 1:14 in the Greek form; the Didache's argument depends on the Greek word "sacrifice," where the Hebrew has "offering."
views.N: "Break bread" on the first day of the week (Acts 20:7); reconciliation before the offering (Matthew 5:23-24); "the Lord's day" (Revelation 1:10).
views.L: Churches read "your sacrifice" differently, from the sacrifice of praise to the offering of the Eucharist; the site's cards at Malachi 1, Luke 22 and Hebrews 10 give the views, and those at Revelation 1 and Acts 20 ask about Sunday and how often to celebrate.

echoes: Revelation 1:10; Acts 20:7; Matthew 5:23-24; Malachi 1:11; Malachi 1:14; Hebrews 13:15; 1 Corinthians 11:18-22

settings.by: The writer of the church order
settings.why: To fix the weekly gathering and to keep it pure by confession and reconciliation, with Malachi as the reason. Knowing the hearers were Gentiles explains the appeal to "my name ... among the nations."
settings.readers: The whole baptized assembly gathered on the Lord's day, including members with quarrels still to settle (14:2).

title: Overseers, deacons and correction
sum: "So choose for yourselves overseers and deacons who are worthy of the Lord": gentle men, free from the love of money, truthful and tested, "for they too perform for you the service of the prophets and teachers." Do not look down on them. Correct one another in peace, "the way you have it in the good news," and have nothing to do with one who wrongs another until he repents. Do your prayers, alms and all your deeds as you have it in the Lord's good news.

views.H: The chapter shows local leaders, several overseers with deacons, being chosen by the community and taking over the work of prophets and teachers. It names no single overseer over a church.
views.N: Philippians 1:1 has "overseers and deacons"; 1 Timothy 3 gives similar qualities; Acts 14:23 uses the same verb for choosing elders; Matthew 18:15-17 the rule of correction.
views.L: Who chooses church leaders, and whether overseers form a separate order from elders, are asked in the site's cards at Acts 14, Acts 20, Philippians 1 and 1 Timothy 3.

echoes: Philippians 1:1; 1 Timothy 3:1-13; Acts 14:23; Matthew 18:15-17; Galatians 6:1; Matthew 6:1-18

settings.by: The writer of the church order
settings.when: Whenever leaders are needed and when members wrong each other
settings.why: To give the community settled leaders of good character and to have it honor them alongside the prophets and teachers, while keeping discipline gentle. It shows a church in change from traveling to local ministry.
settings.readers: Communities that had prophets and teachers but were now choosing their own overseers and deacons.

title: Stay awake: the last days
sum: "Stay awake over your life." Keep your lamps lit and be ready, for you do not know the hour of the Lord's coming. Gather often, for faith counts only if you are made perfect at the end. In the last days false prophets multiply, sheep turn into wolves, love into hate; the world-deceiver appears "as a son of God" with signs and wonders; humankind enters the fire of testing, and those who hold out "will be saved by the curse itself." Then the signs of the truth: something spread out in the sky, a trumpet, and a resurrection, "But not of all the dead": "The Lord will come, and all the saints with him." "Then the world will see the Lord coming on the clouds of the sky." Here the manuscript stops.

views.H: The chapter draws on Matthew 24 and on Jewish apocalyptic hope. The Greek manuscript stops at 16:8; the Georgian version and the Apostolic Constitutions go on to the judgment (Kraft).
views.N: Almost every line has a parallel in Matthew 24-25, 2 Thessalonians 2 and 1 Thessalonians 4; 16:7 quotes Zechariah 14:5 in its Greek form.
views.J: The coming of the Lord with his holy ones (Zechariah 14:5) and the resurrection of the righteous are Jewish hopes taken up by the church.
views.L: The call to gather often (16:2) ties the church's weekly meeting to the hope of the Lord's coming.

deep.b: The Didache counts three "signs of the truth": "the sign of something spread out in the sky," "the sign of a trumpet's sound," and "a resurrection of the dead." The second and third follow Matthew 24:31 and 1 Thessalonians 4:16. The first is Matthew's "sign of the Son of Man" in the sky (Matthew 24:30), given a name: ekpetasis, a spreading out. It can be read as the cross, with arms outstretched (Kraft points to the Ethiopic Apocalypse of Peter and the Epistle of the Apostles, where the cross goes before the coming Lord), or as the sky opened. The resurrection is "not of all," only of the saints who come with the Lord.

The one complete Greek manuscript stops at 16:8, with the rest of the page left blank. Kraft: "both Georg and ApCo lack the words 'of heaven' and continue with a reference to the final judgment," and his translation follows the Georgian ending: "... with power and dominion to repay each man according to his work, with justice, before all men and angels. Amen." The Apostolic Constitutions continues with the Lord coming "with a great concussion above the clouds" to condemn the devil, and ends: "Then shall the wicked go away into everlasting punishment, but the righteous shall go into life eternal" (book 7, chapter 32, in the Ante-Nicene Fathers translation). Kraft also allows that the Didache "should end as in MS H, without further reference to judgment." So the Georgian gives one ending a version knew; whether the Greek original had it is not settled.

echoes: Matthew 24:4-31; Matthew 25:13; Luke 12:35; 2 Thessalonians 2:3-10; 1 Thessalonians 4:16; Zechariah 14:5; Daniel 7:13; Barnabas 4:9

settings.what: The warning about the last days
settings.by: The writer of the church order
settings.when: As the close of the book
settings.why: To end the manual with watchfulness: the rules of the community are kept in the light of the Lord's coming, and the warnings about false prophets in chapter 11 become part of the end-time picture.
settings.readers: The whole community, told to gather often (16:2) and to watch for the Lord's coming.
